speechtext:
Has the Canadian National Railways Company reconsidered its decision to suspend during the
summer months, and to continue every second and third day during the winter season, the service between Edmundston and Levis (trains No. 67, 70 and 68, 69) with a view to providing a regular daily year-round service for the large population of the entire region?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: C.N.R.-SERVICE BETWEEN EDMUNDSTON, N.B. AND LEVIS, QUE.
speechtext:
The management of the Canadian National Railways has sent me the following information:
There was a day coach service three times a week during the winter and the autumn of 1961. In December 1961, a complete train service was re-established. From Montreal this train had a sleeping car connecting with the ocean limited at Levis. Passengers using this service were few and most of them got on at Edmundston. There were also few passengers picked up from intermediate points in the areas of Charny and of Monk. As there had been so few passengers last winter and in the light of a careful analysis of the market possibilities for this winter, a semi-weekly service has been established between Edmundston and Levis with connection for passengers going to Montreal. Traffic on this service will be carefully considered and any future service or changes will be made according to the traffic potential of those trains.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES, PINE POINT RAILWAY
FREIGHT RATES, PINE POINT RAILWAY
speechtext: Do the provisions under which the Pine Point railway is to operate ensure that upon its completion carlot shipments from eastern Canada will have applied to them the one and one third transcontinental rate structure that applies to destinations in Alberta and, if so, what will he (using present tariff) the rate per 100 lbs. on (a) minimum carlots canned vegetables, Toronto-Hay river (b) carlot furniture, Toronto-Hay river?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: FREIGHT RATES, PINE POINT RAILWAY
speechtext:
The management of Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
The Great Slave lake railway is under construction and the projected estimated completion date is the fall of 1966 at which time, when it is in full operation, it will be subject to the then existing statutes and regulations of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada covering the operation of such railways. As a matter of information, section 337 of the Railway Act defines "eastern territory" as any point on a line of railway east of Port Arthur, Ontario or Armstrong, Ontario; "western territory" as any point on a line of railway in British Columbia to which competitive transcontinental tolls apply, and "intermediate territory" as any point between eastern and western territory on any line of railway.
The provisions of this section of the act stipulate that rates to intermediate territory shall not exceed by more than one third the competitive toll in effect to eastern or western territory.
Generally speaking, as destinations on the Pine Point railway qualify under the term "intermediate territory" the effective rates, if that railway were today in operation, would be those within the scope of one and one third of any applicable transcontinental competitive rate.

speechtext:
1.	Has the government a national policy with regard to water and air pollution and, if so, what are the guide lines of such policy?
2.	What steps does the government take to implement its policy?

maintopic: POLICY RESPECTING WATER AND AIR POLLUTION
speechtext:
1. The primary responsibility for the control of air and water pollution rests with the provinces except in the case of international pollution problems and those arising from interprovincial railway systems and shipping within Canadian waters.
The federal government actively participates in studies of international and national significance through the provision of laboratory services, expert consultative service, technical assistance and financial aid under the national health grants program. The federal government also provides loans for municipal sewage treatment projects to abate water pollution as authorized under the National Housing Act.
2. The federal government implements its policy by the adoption of recommendations of the international joint commission. Regulations for the control of air pollution from railway locomotives are formulated by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and regulations for the control of water pollution by oil, by the Department of Transport.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: Could the minister inform the house of any developments concerning the international cooperation year that has been proposed by India at the United Nations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL CO-OPERATION YEAR    REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Sherbrooke for giving me notice of his question. I know of the great interest he has taken in United Nations affairs, having served with distinction a few weeks ago as a Canadian observer.
The house will be interested to know that the general assembly of the United Nations in plenary session this morning unanimously adopted by a vote of 86 in favour, none against and with no abstentions, a resolution cosponsored by India, Canada and 18 other member states in pursuance of a proposal first advanced at the United Nations by Prime Minister Nehru for a year of international co-operation. The Canadian delegation played an active part in the drafting and sponsoring of this resolution, and extended its full cooperation to the delegation of India in seeking to muster the broadest possible support for it.
Inquiries of the Ministry As a matter of fact, by arrangement between the co-sponsors only Canada and India spoke to the resolution this morning.
The resolution requests the president of the general assembly to nominate a preparatory committee of up to 12 member states to consider the desirability of designating 1965, which is the 20th year of the United Nations, as international co-operation year. It is expected that the preparatory committee will be formed early in the new year to begin coordinating plans and projects. It is considered that the designation of a year of international co-operation would serve a most useful purpose in stimulating a marked increase in the existing level of international co-operation and in a number of projects in diverse fields jointly undertaken on an international basis.
Canada firmly subscribes to these aims, and it is therefore a cause of deep satisfaction that the proposal of the government of India to which this government has lent its full support has now been unanimously adopted by the general assembly of the United Nations.

subtopic: COASTAL TRADE
speechtext: I have a question for the Minister of Transport. subtopic: COASTAL TRADE
speechtext:
It is the intention that ships of commonwealth registry which were engaged solely or principally in the Canadian coasting trade in the proposed limited area before the government announced its intention a year and a half ago will be permitted to transfer to Canadian registry.

Mr. Chairman, last evening when talking on the physical fitness program I pointed out that politics had entered into this program. It is very, very difficult to understand why the governor in council was given the power to select the members of the national fitness board. My reason for

raising this matter is that I feel it has put the ministers in a very, very ticklish position; I do not care who the minister is. Also there is no doubt that these men have been put in a ticklish position. When I was at the Canadian sports council I was talking with Dr. Willard, the deputy minister of welfare and I made a suggestion on behalf of the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association. He had received this suggestion from other associations and individual sportsmen, The suggestion was that the national athletic associations would send to the government one or two names of men of known executive ability from those associations, and then the government could make a selection from those names.
There is a definite feeling, no matter what is said on this question, that when a minister has to make a decision it is going to be controversial. But if they had accepted these names of men of outstanding executive ability in the field of sports, nobody could have said that politics was being played in any way, shape or form. I go further than that. I think one of the most flagrant episodes in this connection is this, and I am sorry the minister is not here because it was reported in this house. I refer to the time when the Minister of Public Works, the former minister of justice, toured western Canada. When he was there he gave a partial assurance to the Trail Smoke Eaters hockey club that he would assist them by means of a grant. Mr. Chairman, there is a definite procedure in national sports associations whereby any group, individual or team can make representations through their sports association, which submits it to the national sports fitness group.
That is the only way to do it. There is no doubt we are all put on the spot and it will become a regular schemozzle if every member in this house or the ministers in this house were going after the national sports council and asking them to do something for their constituencies. We certainly do not want that on either side of the house, I am sure. I hope we will have intestinal fortitude enough that when our constituents and people representing teams come to us we shall be able to say: "Look, this has nothing to do with politics. Go to the right source." This is a national project which is absolutely necessary in this country. I know both sides are working in sincerity in order to put this over in a big way, because we need this program.
I should like to make a comment with regard to the structural part. Some of the grants which have been given out to teams

and organizations have been justified, but a great many have not been justified and could not in any circumstances come under a physical fitness program. I do not want to give a long list, but just think of the Canadian rugby team which went over and toured England, Scotland and Ireland. They were given a donation of some $10,000 and I should like to ask the minister: what did that $10,000 do toward improving national fitness in Canada? I know he will say that such a tour makes for good relations and that they have done a good job. I agree 100 per cent, but that is not the job of a national fitness program.
A national fitness program starts with the kids. We can look to Europe and see that this is true. One thing we lack is facilities. Facilities are the main part of any national program. When I was in Ottawa at a meeting of the Canadian Sports Advisory Council some time ago I suggested to them that before they went into this matter of physical fitness they should send a delegation to the countries in Europe which have successful programs. They said they had looked into this and had a satisfactory answer to it. All I will say is this: at that time they definitely had no program. When we think of facilities we think of indoor facilities and outdoor facilities. When we think of indoor facilities we think of rinks and swimming pools. When we think of swimming pools we think of little Mary Stewart in Vancouver, a girl who has made a real contribution and put Canada's name at the top of the list. Do you know how little Mary Stewart had to practice? She practised in pools that were not long enough. Any swimmer knows that when they make the turns they take their breath and after these short swimming pools she was unable to adjust herself when she got into the longer pool of Olympic standards. As far as I know there are something like three pools built to Olympic standard in Canada. I am not sure if there are any indoors for use during the winter. If we are to have outstanding athletes they must have a program for the full season.
Whether we like it or not, during peacetime our country is judged by the prestige of our athletes. I think of little Czechoslovakia, a country of twelve and a half million people where they have had a physical fitness program going for some hundred years. I think we might well go over there to give some study to this program, a program so successful that they have walked away with the gold medals, the silver medals and the bronze medals in Olympic competition. And where has Canada been? I know that many hon. members are thinking I am talking about countries behind the iron curtain. Last night I mentioned Russia. I should like to mention 27507-3-1791
Interim Supply
West Germany. West Germany is a democratic country like our own. West Germany was ravished during the war. When I was over there two years ago, do hon. members know what they had on their program for facilities. They had what they call their golden plan, their 15-year plan. Do hon. members know what that 15-year plan means? It means $1,500 million toward facilities. Yet this government gave $5 million and then took away $4 million-this in a country which the Minister of Finance tells us is a country of prosperity. Then they squelch out $4 million toward a physical fitness program. I have asked a number of questions, some starred questions and others just questions, which have been answered. This is one of the questions which was asked. I asked: if this was a nation-wide organization, what about the province of Quebec? Where did they come into the picture? So far as I have noticed, the province of Quebec does not belong to the national organization. We should like to know more about the reasons for that.
Talking about facilities, we asked the question what amount of money was spent on the facilities? The answer came: the winter works program. Thank goodness for the winter works program. I want to commend the winter works program for the part it is playing. Those responsible for it are doing a grand job but because of the circumstances they can only do so much. How does that program work? It works through the local municipalities who have the get up and go. The ones who have that are the ones who get the rinks, sports fields or whatever they may be. But what about those sections which are afraid or unable to put up that extra money? The kids in those sections probably need the facilities a great deal more than the kids in the sections where people are up and doing. Is the program doing anything for them? We need every cent of those $5 million to start this off.
Just as important as facilities is coaching. The Canadian hockey association under Mr. Gordon Jukes as secretary manager got in touch with the universities of Canada to try to form a summer school for coaching college courses. He really received co-operation. It was brought up before the council, and I am pleased to see that the council is backing it. I sincerely hope that when it passes the final word along the government will go along with it.
It is the lack of facilities and coaching which causes us to lose our youth of today to our neighbour across the line. Mr. Chairman, last year it was my privilege to be in Colorado Springs with our hockey club. There I met a lot of former young Canadians who

Interim Supply
were graduates from the universities of the United States. They had to go there because there were no facilities here in Canada. They did not have any coaching at all in Canada, and because they had ability in running, or in swimming, or in playing hockey, the universities of the United States took them and have kept them.
And they can keep them too.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: What did your government do for them?
Never mind that. It is not what has been done; it is what is to be done right now.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think it is a rule of this committee that only one member can have the floor at one time, and at the present time the hon. member for Norfolk has the floor.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

There is another angle to this physical fitness question which perhaps many of us do not realize. The physical fitness program can serve a double purpose. It can go far beyond the question of fitness.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

If my hon. friend over there would listen, I think he would agree with me. We have records showing that in every community where there have been no minor sports organizations, and where minor sport organizations were organized; with every increase in registration in these minor sports organizations less delinquency has resulted. I do not know whether hon. members realize the alarming increase in our penitentiaries population. Dominion-wise, in 1957 it was 5,400; in 1962 it was 7,200. The federal government is building five new prisons costing $4 million each. What disturbs me, and it should disturb every member of this committee, is that three of these penitentiaries are for the youth of Canada. It costs us $21 million, and the province of Ontario alone $16 million. We cannot afford not to organize youth. Each department of government looks after its own dollars and cents, and has possibly overlooked the true value to our nation of a properly run physical fitness program. When you add to this the development of moral fibre through sports activities, the returns our young men and women will get from it in the future cannot be assessed in dollars and cents. It goes far beyond that.

Very few people outside of entertainment really realize what sports mean. In closing I should like to illustrate the very great importance of sport, what it means to this country and to the countries of the world. As we know, sport is one of the main by-products of any fitness program. I could give many illustrations of this but it would take too long. The greatest medium of all for breaking down barriers is sport. It is the common denominator of all creeds and religions. It does not make any difference whether we are Jews, Catholics or Protestants. It does not make any difference whether we are black, white or yellow. When young men and women go on to the sports field within their communities within our country, and also in international competition, they are as one.
I should like to leave this thought with the committee, and especially with our enlightening friend across the way. I should like, not on behalf of the Liberal opposition party or other opposition members on behalf of any members with common sense on that side of the house to ask the Prime Minister and his executive to think twice about taking away this sum of $5 million. Because the youth of Canada-and I am speaking for the youth of Canada-are the most important members of the Canadian family; I hope everyone will agree with that. We should give more serious consideration to retaining this sum of $5 million so that the national fitness program will go, not only a long way towards the program itself but also will go a long way towards strengthening the moral fibre of our nation.

council. It is this council which was set up. I should like to ask him this question. Does he think that the governor in council was playing politics when Mr. James Worrall was appointed to this council?

Mr. Chairman, may I answer the first question first. You will remember that at the beginning of my remarks I said that the Prime Minister had made a statement at the opening of the hockey hall of fame about a $5 million grant. I also pointed out that only under the present government would such a thing happen. Because when any businessman, small or big, goes to borrow money, he takes a plan with him. The only reason why this money is not being spent, and the only reason why it cannot be spent, is because the government has no plan for spending the money. We can certainly show the government where to spend this money, and spend it in a big way.
As far as Mr. Worrall is concerned, I agree with the minister. I will not answer any questions except to say that you put your ministers in one dickens of a spot. But I do know this, that if you had had a program you would be able to spend your $5 million. Germany has spent $1.5 billion on facilities alone. Has the government an answer to that?

Mr. Chairman, I readily endorse the remarks made yesterday by my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), and those made by all hon. members who took part in this debate on national unity. As a matter of fact, I should like to repeat what I said in this house a few weeks ago:
Interim Supply
As everybody knows, Canada was founded to a great extent by two distinct nations, and our country will come to its fullest expression only if the equality of the French and English languages and cultures is recognized in fact as well as in law throughout the country.
Mr. Chairman, the leader of the New Democratic party did not hesitate to point out that fact and to remind the house of the recommendation he made last February when he advocated the establishment of a royal commission to look into this fundamental question. It gives us very great satisfaction to note that all parties represented in this house agree on the necessity of putting an end to the uneasiness affecting national unity and of casting aside demagogic and unpatriotic politics which threaten Canada's future.
Mr. Chairman, like all Canadian citizens, I hope that the spirit pervading this debate will survive the next election campaign. With all sincere Canadians, I hope that nobody will attempt to take political advantage of the present situation, but instead that all will strive to advocate firm unity throughout Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I urge the Prime Minister to introduce without delay the legislation tending to set up that royal commission which all those who took part in this debate seem to be asking for.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, this is the most suitable time to act along these lines. We must not wait until tension increases to the breaking point. We must not wait any more to make the historic move which will enable Canada, I am sure, to strengthen its ties so as to present to the whole world, when the confederation centennial will be celebrated in 1967, the best possible example of unity and understanding between two equal races, which are partners in the development and progress of one of the richest and most beautiful countries in the world.
I repeat that the time to act has come. At a time when all parties agree on that matter, it is up to the Prime Minister to make now the historic move that is requested by everybody.
(Text):
I should like, before going on to the major subject of my remarks, to say a few words in English on the subject, and deliberately in English, with respect to a gentleman in Hamilton and with respect to an organization recently set up in the province of Quebec. I refer to a man of the cloth in the city of Hamilton who had the bad grace and the lack

Interim Supply
of understanding of Canada to raise objections, expressed in violent language, against the teaching of French in the schools of the province of Ontario, and I say: Shame to him and to others like him in English speaking Canada.
I also draw the attention of the house to the few noisy separatists in the province of Quebec who have recently formed what they call a political organization for the purpose of tearing Quebec away from Canada and establishing what they call the republic of Quebec. It is these two extremes in our country, fortunately representing relatively few people in both sections of Canada, who cause so much trouble. It is against those people and their influence that a royal commission of inquiry could once and for all establish the kind of harmony to which everyone who has spoken in this chamber looks forward for our country.
I turn from this to a related world problem. I turn from the conception which has been underlined by the Leader of the Opposition in noble and appropriate words and underlined by my leader in equally appropriate words, the proposition of the equality of the two major nations in Canada-and all other groups as I am sure the Leader of the Opposition and my leader would agree-to the astounding attitude of our government. I refer to its policy with respect to the treatment which is now meted out on the continent of Africa by the government of the Union of South Africa, and by the government and forces of Portugal, to the African people under their rule and under their control.
I remind the house of the fact that, in answer to questions, the Prime Minister some days ago stated with respect to South Africa that this country was not going to honour a request by the United Nations resolution for an economic boycott of South Africa because, said he, we do some $40 million or $50 million worth of trade with South Africa and therefore we are not going to cut it off. I remind the committee also of the fact that in recent days Canada abstained from voting on a resolution condemning Portugal for its treatment of the African people in the west African territories under its administration, and that only yesterday, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs informed us earlier, Canada opposed a similar resolution of condemnation of Portugal because of its barbaric and inhuman behaviour toward the Africans in Angola. He said that the resolution was too extreme for Canada to swallow and digest.
I have a copy of the resolution in my hand, Mr. Chairman. The minister said the resolution suggested that Portugal was going to be thrown out of the United Nations. With great respect, I do not see that in the resolution,

and may I make clear that neither my colleagues nor I favour the expulsion of any member of the United Nations. We favour the United Nations being all-inclusive. What this resolution does is to remind the government of Portugal that her continued non-implementation of the resolutions of the general assembly and the security council-these are resolutions relating to territories under Portuguese control-is inconsistent with her membership in the United Nations.
What can be more clear than that the kind of barbarism, the kind of racialism, the kind of oppression which the Portuguese government is now carrying on in Angola and other territories under its control is indeed inconsistent with membership in the United Nations, a membership which accepts the propositions in the charter of the United Nations and in the declaration on human rights?
The minister said that Canada could not swallow the suggestion of sanctions. May I put on the record, Mr. Chairman, what the resolution says on that score? The resolution requests the security council to take appropriate measures, including sanctions, to secure Portugal's compliance with this resolution. That is the Portuguese resolution of the general assembly and of the security council. I ask, what could be a more reasonable request on the part of the assembly than that the security council, the executive arm of the United Nations, take appropriate steps, including sanctions, to assure that Portugal will comply with her obligations under the United Nations charter.
What we have, Mr. Chairman, I suggest- and I do not for one moment apologize for using the rather strong language I am about to use-is a statement by the leaders in the government of our country that because of $40 million or $50 million worth of trade with South Africa, because of the fact Portugal is a member of NATO and we are a member of NATO, we are prepared to abandon the basic principles on which democracy is founded and upon which this country is founded, and throw to the wolves the concepts of human rights, human equality and human dignity. We are prepared to do this in order to hold $40 million or $50 million worth of trade with South Africa and in order to enable our fellow member in NATO, Portugal, to have arms. There cannot be any greater condemnation of the policies of NATO in the eyes of the uncommitted peoples of the world than the excuse that because Portugal is a member of NATO we are going to supply it with arms and other military equipment, so that country can continue its oppression of the African people in its territories.

Where is the moral leadership in the world today, Mr. Chairman? I have looked carefully into some of the reports coming out of South Africa. Everyone here has already read the reports coming out of Angola and other Portuguese territories. I want to put on the record, Mr. Chairman, certain words which I wish could be inscribed indelibly on the minds and hearts of all the leaders of the western nations. The following are the words of Nelson Mandela, lieutenant of chief Albert Lutuli in South Africa, a Nobel prize winner who has been virtually under detention by the government. Mr. Mandela was in court on various charges and was making a defence of his actions before the court. In the course of that defence he said this:
Through bitter experience, we have learned to regard the white man as a harsh and merciless type of human being whose contempt for our rights, and whose utter indifference to the promotion of our welfare, makes his assurances to us absolutely meaningless and hypocritical.
I say to hon. members of this house, Mr. Chairman, and I plead with the government, that our attitude on South Africa, our attitude on Portugal, our attitude to these governments which deny and destroy the concept of human rights, of human dignity in the countries over which they rule, is wrong and unwise, especially in the light of the statement by Mr. Mandela that our assurances to them are absolutely meaningless and hypocritical. If the western nations of the world want to win the support and confidence of the African peoples and the Asian peoples, it is time we abandoned the ruthless mercantilism which is implied in the answer of the Prime Minister and the ruthless militarism which is implied in the answer of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and acted in accordance with the principles set out in the preamble to the bill of rights of which the Prime Minister is so proud.
Let me remind hon. members what we said in this parliament:
The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions;
Affirming also that men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law;
I ask, Mr. Chairman, what moral and spiritual values is this government defending when it refuses to take action in concert with other nations of the United Nations to punish South Africa and Portugal for their oppression of human beings in their territories and to find some way of changing the policies in those lands.
Interim Supply
What is happening in South Africa? Mr. Mandela, to whom I have referred, in his speech to the court described in these words the situation in which he found himself:
I found myself trailed by officers of the security branch of the police force wherever I went. In short I found myself treated as a criminal, an unconvicted criminal. I was not allowed to pick my company, to frequent the company of men, to participate in their political activities, to join their organizations. I was not free from constant police surveillance any more than a convict in one of our jails is free from surveillance. I was made, by the law, a criminal, not because of what I had done, but what I stood for, because of what I thought, because of my conscience. Can it be any wonder to anybody that such conditions make a man an outlaw of society?
According to an article in the London Observer, Mr. Chairman, during the month of May 1962, prior to the proclamation of South Africa as a republic, almost 10,000 Africans were arrested in house raids throughout the country. The ostensible reason was to avoid republican day agitation. Also to the same end, ostensibly the government rushed through the house in less than one week the general law amendment act. This general law amendment act gave magistrates the right to refuse bail for 12 days; gave magistrates the right to refuse a trial by jury and shifted the onus on the accused to prove his innocence, contrary to the basic principles for which we stand.
They do that in France.

France is an entirely different story. The hon. gentleman says they do this in France, but he is wrong. What they do in France, and in other countries of Europe, is that they have an entirely different system of the enforcement of law; they have various investigations and inquiries that make their system whole. In South Africa they pretend to have our system of justice and under our system of justice it is considered an injustice, cruel and undemocratic, to place the onus upon the accused to prove his innocence.
In April, 1962, the tension in South Africa is reported to have increased to the extent that South Africa built up its defence apparatus, mainly its permanent force, security police, and armed services for the purpose of suppressing an armed revolt. Then, last May I believe it was, Mr. Chairman, or perhaps in June, they passed what is known as the sabotage bill. By all accounts, this is the most vicious piece of legislation of its kind since Hitler's Germany. This is the country with which we say we are going to continue to trade because of the $40 million or $50 million of trade that is involved.
The London Observer said in an editorial at the end of May that from now on the conflict will assume its true Hitlerian character.

Under this act sabotage has been defined as injury or damage to property, and even obstructing traffic. The penalties tor these as well as more serious offences is the death sentence, or a minimum compulsory five years imprisonment. It applies to juveniles as well as to adults and, according to the act, there is no appeal.
I think it is important to set these matters on record because as I watch what is happening in Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and other western nations today, with respect to South Africa and Portugal, I am reminded of what happened in the thirties. In 1935, I returned to this country after an absence of three years during which time I among many other people visited Germany, and met many Canadians who listened to our stories as to what was happening in Germany. Even though it might have penetrated their minds they did not let it penetrate their hearts because, like decent people everywhere, they found it impossible to believe that men could act in so inhuman a fashion as the nazis were acting in Germany. It was only after the war ended that they realized there indeed was a regime that was barbaric and inhuman, which took millions of people into the gas chamber, which did destroy human beings because of difference in colour or religion, and which did have all the vicious tendencies we who visited Germany had talked about in the thirties.
At that time people in Canada and elsewhere, people with good minds and good character, and who lived in free societies, found it difficult to believe those things were happening; but today in the same way the white world, the western nations, are making precisely the same mistake one would have thought they would once have learned to avoid. They are making the mistake of not believing that white people, such as the government of South Africa, could be guilty of such things and that Portugal could be guilty of them.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is one of the finest and gentlest human beings I have had the pleasure of meeting; yet he says in all honesty, and I am sure in all integrity, that he sat beside the minister representing Portugal at the NATO council meeting and was impressed that there were two sides to the question. His words were "more than one side". Mr. Chairman, there cannot be two sides to cruelty; there cannot be two sides to barbarism; there cannot be two sides to inhumanity. There is only one side. It is evil; it ought to be punished, and every assembly in the civilized world ought to take action against it. I am ashamed that

a minister of the government of my country should be able to see two sides in such a matter.
In my submission economic sanctions are now, as they have been throughout the years, one of the major weapons short of war in the hands of the agencies of collective security. I suggest there is really no other weapon of coercion; and I frankly admit it is a weapon of coercion, short of war, when all attempts at persuasion have failed to achieve the purposes sought.
The attitude of the government with respect to South Africa and Portugal reminds me, and I am sure all hon. members here will remember it as I recall the story, of the time in 1935 when Dr. Riddell, one of the representatives of Canada at the league of nations in Geneva, appointed by the Liberal government before 1930 and who served during the Bennett regime from 1930 to 1935, committed this country to oil sanctions against Italy because of its invasion of Ethiopia. Then the government which came in in October of that year repudiated Dr. Riddell through the mouths of gentlemen like the late Mr. Lapointe and Mr. Mackenzie King.
Now once again we are great collective securitists, great supporters of the United [DOT]Nations and of the idea of the United Nations, but only until such time as we have to take an action which may jeopardize several million dollars worth of our trade, or until such time as we have to take an action which may hurt the military status of one of the members of NATO.
I	say that the government in October, 1935, betrayed the league of nations and its purposes, and the government of this country today, together with the governments of other countries with which we are allied, are now betraying the purposes of the United Nations and the purposes of the charter of the United Nations by our attitude toward these things in South Africa, Angola and other African territories under the administration of Portugal.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that when the question of economic sanctions was discussed in the political commission of the United Nations, Mr. Duma Nokwe, former secretary general of the African national congress, now banned, replied to the position taken by Mr. Crowes, the United Kingdom delegate, who had said that sanctions would hurt the Africans more than it would hurt those supporting apartheid. Mr. Duma Nokwe said:

of the problems of South Africa and of creating the atmosphere for bloodshed and chaos ... The only way-
And I commend this to hon. members-
-of teaching the whites that racialist policies must be abandoned is by removing the economic benefits which they think they get from this system. It is fallacious to suggest that if economic sanctions were imposed on South Africa the nonwhites would suffer most.
The Reverend Michael Scott, who was a South African and was banned by the South African government, writing in the Observer of recent issue said that the trend to violence woud unleash "a holocaust of hatred the like of which has not been seen anywhere in Africa or Asia."
I regret this kind of comment has to be made on interim supply instead of on a debate on external affairs, and I am sorry this has to be the case. I suggest that if western nations are not careful, the moral leadership of the world will be given to the new nations of Asia and Africa, and these people who have reason to suspect us and resent our behaviour in the past will be ripe for communist dogma and communist solutions of their problems. Part of our weaponry against communist expansion is steadfast support of the rights of nations to independence, and steadfast support for the equality of all men, white black or yellow and, no matter what the cost, we should not waver in our support of those basic principles.
Nelson Mandela, to whom I have already referred, said in his speech, and I commend his noble words to everyone in this chamber:
I hate the practice of race discrimination, and in doing so, in my hatred, I am sustained by the fact that the overwhelming majority of mankind hates it equally. I hate the systematic inculcation of children with colour prejudice and I am sustained in that hatred by the fact that the overwhelming majority of mankind, here and abroad, are with me in that. I hate the racial arrogance which decrees that the good things of life shall be retained as the exclusive right of a minority of the population, and which reduces the majority of the population to a subservience and inferiority, and maintains them as voteless chattels to work where they are told and behave as they are told by the ruling minority.
Nothing that this court can do to me will change in any way that hatred in me, which can only be removed by the removal of the injustice and the inhumanity which I have sought to remove from the political, social and economic life of this country.
Mr. Chairman, I say that when we have fought to uphold the ideas that Mr. Mandela- a lawyer trained, if I am correct in my memory, in Britain-took from us, it is our duty, we who have spread these ideas or at least helped to spread them, to give them a reality in the lives of the people of Africa. I say, Mr. Chairman, of what value is it to belong to the United Nations, to proclaim the charter of the United Nations, to be a signatory to the declaration of human rights, to boast of our presence in that international body, to speak of its importance to the world-of what use is all that if, when the United Nations adopts a resolution requiring economic sanctions against a country, we ignore it because it may hurt our trade a little; and when the United Nations adopts a resolution requiring economic sanctions against another country, we ignore it because we happen to be in a military alliance with that country. Mr. Chairman, this discussion on interim supply has roamed far and wide. Indeed, I have taken part in the roaming myself and I make no apology for that. If I speak again, it is to deal with a specific matter arising out of the request for interim supply. But I think it should be pointed out that, while the discussion of this matter has roamed far and wide, some very important matters have been brought before the house which could not have been brought before the house in any other way at this time.
Mr. Chairman, we met in late September instead of in early August, and since we met the business of this house has been arranged in such a way that many of the most urgent questions could not be debated in the way in which they should have been debated. This requires that these matters should be raised in the kind of discussion that we are having this week. Some of the matters brought forth in this discussion could well have been brought forth as parts of separate debates dealing with them if the house had been so organized and if we had had time to debate some of the important matters that

Interim Supply
have now been raised. For instance, the failure of the government to formulate policy in the field of transportation; the failure of the government to have trade policy discussed in the house in order to ascertain how long term solutions to the different problems of international trade could be achieved; the accusations or charges that are being made that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are making unwarranted investigations into the political opinions of individual citizens; the failure of the government to bring forth for discussion in this house the Columbia river treaty; the failure of the government to develop and enunciate a defence policy; the failure of the government to make it possible for us to have a debate on foreign affairs so that we could discuss within the context of such a debate the important matters for instance, that have just been raised by my hon. friend who has just spoken; the failure of the government to deal constructively with the problems of eastern agriculture. These are matters that require separate debate in this house. Because we have not been able to organize our business so that could be done, and because we did not meet, as we should have met, earlier this summer, we have had to take advantage of this kind of motion in order to bring these matters to the attention of the house in the hope that government spokesmen would deal with them in replying to the points made by spokesmen from the opposition. I believe I am right in saying that none of the points I have mentioned-and there have been others-has been dealt with in any way by any spokesman on behalf of the government.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we find ourselves in a position-I think I am using the words of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre- where the government has got itself boxed in, in a parliamentary sense, in regard to the question of supply. The old parliament granted interim supply for seven months. Twice in this parliament further supply has been granted, each time for one month. I am right in saying that on each occasion interim supply was expedited by the opposition so we could get ahead with other important business which we assumed the government would bring forward. Our assumption and our hopes in that regard were denied by the event. There is, I believe, no precedent in our parliamentary history for a government asking for the tenth monthly instalment of the total expenditures for a year before one single item of annual expenditure has been voted by parliament- not one. This is something that has not happened before in our parliamentary history.
Whose fault is it?
We will soon find out whose fault it is.
Yes, let us find out.

It is a traditional and fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they are collected and to approve expenditures before they are made. When these rights are ignored, when they are violated, parliament itself is being violated and we are taking a step toward its destruction. No matter how wide a circulation we give and no matter in what form, to the bill of rights, and no matter how much we may talk about Magna Carta and the bill of rights, no matter how emotionally we may wrap ourselves up in parliamentary or national flags, both these rights I have mentioned are being deliberately and systematically violated by the present government. New rates of taxation recommended in the budget last April have been collected for over eight months without parliamentary approval. Taxes of an annual value of $200 million, imposed by order in council- an order in council of doubtful legal and constitutional validity and about which we cannot get the legal opinion on which it was based-have been collected for six months. Every effort we have made to bring these taxes before parliament for approval or for rejection has been frustrated and refused.
Now in this bill we are asked to give the government a cheque for another one-twelfth of our annual expenditure. That would make a total of some $5 billion in blank cheques to this government. Of course, this bill is totally unnecessary. We are considering it only because the government has failed to respect the constitutional rights of the elected representatives of the people. If the government had wished, the government could have secured approval of the annual expenditures and of the tax changes proposed in the last budget before holding a general election. The government chose instead, as was its right, to appeal to the people for a new mandate. They did not receive that mandate. But they exercised that right of appeal to the people before any single estimate had been passed and before there had been a budget debate.
After the election, as has been said before in this house, the government had a right to carry on as a caretaker administration, but only until the earliest date at which parliament could have been summoned. That date would have been the last week in July. Parliament, as we have said on this side, should have met then and the government should have asked at once for a vote of confidence. That question would have been settled under our rules after eight days of debate at the most. If the government had

secured a vote of confidence after eight days it could then have placed the new taxation measures before parliament at once. That could have been done, of course, in a budget which would have contained those long term financial and economic proposals promised by the Prime Minister at that time with great solemnity and with great emphasis, as something which would be introduced at the earliest opportunity to take the place of the emergency proposals which were made at the time the austerity program was announced on June 24 and 25.
If the government had done that, the budget debate would have been limited under our rules to six days. The tax proposals resulting from such a budget would not have taken long to deal with. The revised estimates could have been tabled at once and priority could have been given to the consideration of those estimates in the latter part of August and September. The whole program of taxation and expenditure could have been disposed of by the beginning of October if such a program had been followed by this government and if the government had continued to maintain the confidence of the house. Then October, November and December would have been available to the government for legislation. If the budget and the long term program for dealing with our basic problems had been approved, the session could have been concluded before Christmas, instead of the House of Commons finding itself in the position in which it finds itself now, a position which has been graphically described in the Winnipeg Free Press-I know hon. gentlemen opposite will not like it, but this extract from that newspaper of the day before yesterday describes the situation very accurately. It reads:
Parliament is about to adjourn for its Christmas holidays without coming to grips with any basic Canadian problem.
Then the writer goes on:
Since September the government has blamed the opposition for blockading public business and argued that it could not get on with its major policies of financial and economic reform until the routine agenda was cleared away. It knows, however, that if any major policy were submitted, parliament would consider it without delay. None has been submitted. Parliament will just go home for Christmas with everything of importance postponed.
It is true, of course, that there has been nothing of real general economic importance placed on the order paper so far. The long range economic policies of the government about which the Prime Minister talked so much and so eloquently last June and July-[DOT] where are they? There have been some important features of specific legislation put on the order paper. There is even one which is of some general economic importance, the 27507-3-180i

setting up of a national development board; but that turns out to be less important than some of us had been led to believe. There is nothing on the order paper, and there has been nothing to give us the chance of implementing in any shape or form the long range economic policies of the government which the Prime Minister said were necessary at the time of the emergency and which would replace the emergency austerity program.
If the government had followed the course of calling parliament together at the end of July, if it had managed to organize in an efficient way the business of this house, we would have reached the point by now of having this legislation and these policies in action and we could have come back in the new year conscious, perhaps, that we had been able to do something-if we come back at all.
The Prime Minister and his supporters say we are responsible over here for any delay there has been. They say we have been holding things up. They used that argument last spring as an excuse for going to the country. They ask: why don't you speed up business? Why don't you get ahead? May I point out that we have made three specific and concrete proposals from this side to government spokesmen which would have had the effect of speeding up the progress of the business which is now on the order paper. We have said three things, none of which has been taken up as far as we know. We have agreed to the allocation of time to specific legislation. That would be done by agreement, and it is a very important concession for an opposition to make. We have agreed to a reduction, if it is a reduction to 30 minutes of the time spent on oral questions on orders of the day, and we have agreed to the prolongation of each day's sitting beyond ten o'clock if that should be necessary to complete the current business before the house or the committee of the whole. These are three specific proposals which have been made by this side as an indication of our willingness to get ahead even with the business which the government has on the order paper.

As I have already stated, parliament's examination of, and control over, government spending is the very foundation of our democratic parliamentary system. But this year the estimates of only one department have been brought before parliament. Presumably we will be discussing the rest in February with eleven twelfths of the expenditure already spent. The government will not be explaining or defending its plans and its expenditure. It will be reporting to the house on old history, on what it has already spent. That is the situation in which we now find ourselves when we are asked to vote this further interim supply.
Mr. Chairman, as we have already indicated we on this side are prepared to vote this measure of interim supply in order to enable the business of the country to go on into the new year. speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Public Works) moved
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PERIOD FOR CONSTRUCTION OF SEWAGE TREATMENT PROJECTS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1954 to extend for an additional two years the period within which the construction of a sewage treatment project in respect of which a loan has been or is to be made must be completed if the municipality or municipal corporation is to be granted a reduction of indebtedness.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Chown in the chair.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PERIOD FOR CONSTRUCTION OF SEWAGE TREATMENT PROJECTS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I understand that because of the speed with which we have moved in the last few minutes there will be some little delay in actually getting copies of the bill up here in order that they may be available to hon. members for study when we actually reach that stage. Perhaps I could make a brief statement to explain the purpose of the bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PERIOD FOR CONSTRUCTION OF SEWAGE TREATMENT PROJECTS
speechtext: May I ask the minister if this is his valedictory?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PERIOD FOR CONSTRUCTION OF SEWAGE TREATMENT PROJECTS
speechtext:
No, I shall have even more important things to say in my valedictory.
The purpose of the bill which this legislation precedes is to extend the forgiveness date applicable to federal loans for construction of sewage treatment projects under Part VIB of the National Housing Act.
Hon. members will recall that this program was authorized under an amendment to the National Housing Act passed by parliament in December, 1960. Under this part of the act, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is authorized to make long term, low interest loans to municipalities for the construction and expansion of central treatment or disposal plants or the construction of trunk collector sewers. The loans may be for periods of up to 50 years and for amounts equal to two thirds of the cost of the projects.
The 1960 legislation provided for partial debt cancellation where projects were completed or were under construction by March 31, 1963. In these cases the corporation was authorized to forgive payment of 25 per cent of the amount of the loan advanced, and 25 per cent of the interest accrued on the amount outstanding. The purpose of these provisions was twofold: to provide an incentive to

municipalities to make an early start on these works and to encourage additional employment in construction and allied fields.
In view of the national significance of the program, the government is now asking parliament to extend the effective date of this forgiveness clause by an additional two year period.
I think most of us recognize that one of the most pressing problems of the times is the steady and increasing pollution of our soil and water resources. This not only threatens conservation of the nation's wildlife, it interferes with the fullest possible use of the recreational potential of our streams and rivers and, indeed, in some instances, can and does pose serious health problems. Communities with a high degree of soil and water pollution in their area are concerned about the health hazards that can result from this type of contamination.
The government's intention in introducing the legislation in December, 1960, was to help municipalities strike at the root of the problem by assisting them in providing proper sewage treatment facilities. I need hardly add the failure to provide adequate and sufficient treatment facilities would also interfere with the proper growth and development of a community and might also seriously restrict the provision of adequate housing in many parts of the country.
The lending program has been extremely successful. The 1960 amendment to the act enabled Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make loans for sewage treatment purposes up to an aggregate amount of $100 million. Last December, because of the number of applications already received, the government asked and obtained authorization from parliament to raise this ceiling to $200 million. Since the inception of the program in December, 1960, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has made 360 loans for a total of more than $85 million. In addition, at the end of November, 1962, the corporation had on hand applications or inquiries for 146 loans with a loan potential of $52.5 million.
Loans have been made to municipalities in every part of Canada and to communities of every size, from large metropolitan centres to rural municipalities of less than 1,000 population. Nearly 200 municipalities of less than 5,000 population, have been assisted under this program. Loans have also been made to 62 communities with populations of between 5,000 and 25,000 and to 36 cities with populations in excess of 25,000.
It is true the response has not been uniform in all parts of the country. Although loans have been made to municipalities in every province, the bulk of the lending has
National Housing Act
occurred in two or three provinces, notably Ontario and Saskatchewan. However, applications now on hand show a much wider interest in the use of these facilities. Many other municipalities have indicated their desire to institute effective programs for control of pollution in their area. We have been asked to extend the effective forgiveness date so that municipalities now coming forward with proposals will not be placed at a disadvantage in financing these works.
The government feels that, although we have made considerable progress so far in dealing with the pollution problem, much still remains to be done. Many municipalities face grievous problems and are becoming increasingly aware of the need to take remedial action and of the assistance they can obtain from the federal government. Moreover, it must also be recognized that in some areas and along some waterways not all municipalities have yet taken advantage of the legislation. Thus, although some individual towns and cities have undertaken construction of treatment plants to alleviate the problem in their immediate environment, this alone is not sufficient to restore the purity of the river itself. To do this, all municipalities-both upstream and downstream-must take steps to treat their sewage adequately. For these reasons the government is recommending this further amendment to the act.
Under the terms of the bill to be founded on this resolution, the expiry date will be extended to March 31, 1965 and municipalities will be able to take advantage of the 25 per cent rebate on principal and accrued interest, provided their projects are completed by that date. The rebate, of course, will also apply to projects still in course of construction at that time but the amount of forgiveness will be calculated on the work performed prior to March 31, 1965.
Mr. Chairman, when I say the expiry date will extend to March 31, 1965, that refers to the rebate provision which was to expire on March 31, 1963. The program itself, the loan program to municipalities, as I have explained before, by virtue of the 1960 amendment is a continuing feature of the National Housing Act and will continue whether or not portions of the loan are rebated.
It is clear that many municipalities with work now in hand will be unable to complete their projects by next March. Moreover, several communities are in the process of drawing up plans and specifications and will find it difficult to proceed with operations this winter unless they have some certainty as to the effective forgiveness date. I know hon. members will wish to see this vital

National Housing Act
work expedited, particularly during the offseason months when construction projects can provide substantial additional employment, and that they will consider the bill with the same sense of urgency matching that with which it has been introduced.
I also hope that hon. members will assist not only the government but their municipalities or their regions by drawing to the attention of all municipal and district councils the fact that the rebate provision has now been extended, and thus encourage their municipalities to take advantage of the loan provision as well as the rebate provision.

Mr. Chairman, we on this side have been looking forward to the introduction of this legislation, because some of us were hoping to make contributions to the debate which would normally follow in connection with the National Housing Act and certain aspects of it which we feel could be improved and should be improved at this time. However, in order to co-operate with the government, and in the spirit we have seen during the last half hour in the house, we are willing to forgo that and say our position is exactly the same as I outlined it in the house on November 2 when the minister made the anouncement.
We are most anxious to do whatever we can to co-operate in facilitating the passage of this legislation through the house. Perhaps the minister himself recognizes one of the weaknesses of this particular legislation is the piecemeal aspect of it, covering a year or two at a time. The establishment of a municipal loan fund would enable municipalities which have projects urgently needing to be done to plan years in advance. The people are there to do these projects and we believe that the municipal loan fund, as suggested by my leader more than four years ago, is the answer to helping municipalities. However, I shall deal with that subject on another occasion. All I wish to say now is that we are pleased to co-operate in getting the legislation through the house this afternoon.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PERIOD FOR CONSTRUCTION OF SEWAGE TREATMENT PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to take just one moment also to applaud the extension that the minister has announced today. I believe this certainly shows a much more proper approach to this problem than we have seen in the past. I think the tremendous pressure for this extension that has been generated all across the country should prove to the minister and the government that you cannot deal with problems like this in the ad hoc way that has been used in the past. To do a proper job in this field it has to be done over a long period of time. You cannot expect a one-year program, with all the necessary planning and

preparatory work required, to be as successful as it will be now this extension has been made.
The minister mentioned the successful way in which this fund has been used in the past. I think further successes will be demonstrated over the next two years which will again prove to this government, or whatever government there might happen to be at that time, that this particular program and the method of carrying it out should be broadened and lengthened. It is something that could well become a permanent feature in projects of this nature. Mr. Chairman, I will not take up any more time of the committee. I am also imbued with what seems to be the spirit prevalent in this house today, to get on with the business.

I may say, Mr. Chairman, that little did I think when I listened to the minister's father, who was then a minister in the provincial government of British Columbia, talk about public works-mostly roads at that time-that in 1962 in this house I would listen to his son, who was not then born.
The members of this group support the principle of this resolution and its purpose. We will have a great deal more to say at the appropriate time with respect to further amendments required to the housing act. I was interested in the minister's emphasis on the need to prevent pollution of rivers and the conservation of natural resources. I am sure we are all behind everything the government does in this respect. This also applies to the prevention of destruction of wildlife. Also, I hope he applies that principle to a very large river in my constituency and saves a great deal of the wildlife that is in imminent danger of destruction, if certain things occur.
I rise particularly to mention the plight of a number of small villages in my constituency-some 20 of them-some incorporated, some unincorporated. I presume the same problem occurs in other constituencies. These small villages are on numerous occasions denied the opportunity to obtain loans from the corporation on the ground that they have not

Canadian World Exhibition Corporation
a sewage disposal system. I understand the minister is giving serious consideration to this problem. There are many such villages in Canada, no doubt, which suffer an injustice under this type of ruling. I am going to give one illustration of a small village some few miles from my home. I refer to the village of Nakusp, one of the historic villages of British Columbia. There the site is excellent; there is a depth of 100 feet of sand upon which the village is situated. The drainage is excellent. Everything is ideal for the installation of septic tanks, and generally speaking the home owners have septic tanks. But some people have applied for loans in a subdivision which is an extension of the village and have been denied loans by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation because there is no sewage disposal system.
Villages of this size will not for many years have the financial capacity to construct sewage systems, possibly for generations. I do urge reconsideration of these regulations so that where it can be proved that there is no hazard to water resources, to health and things of that sort, where the site, soil and drainage are satisfactory, these people living in the smaller places in Canada will have the same opportunity to obtain loans as those who live in the larger centres. That is all I have to say, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks on this bill, I wish to point out that in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, they managed to rush the bill through Monday morning. In fact, the committee met at 9.30 a.m. and at 9.32 a.m. the bill had been rushed through although the members had not had time to get there. Things were rushed because it was realized that there was increasing objections to the government interfering with the trucking private enterprise.
Indeed, it was mentioned in the committee that the C.N.R. received each year quite substantial grants to reduce its freight rates while at the same time it entered into competition with private trucking companies.
Freight Rates Reduction Act
That is a strange way of spending public funds. Money is taken from the Canadian taxpayer's pocket and handed over to a crown corporation which uses it to compete with private enterprise.
Mr. Chairman, we protest of course against that policy, all the more since the C.N.R. has entered that field, in the province of Quebec, without securing a permit from the Quebec transport board. And what does the C.N.R. say in reply to such facts? Here it is: We went into that field; proceedings were taken against us before the courts of the province of Qubec; let us wait and see what the courts will decide.
In my opinion, when the federal government allows the C.N.R. to do that, it sets a bad precedent.
Mr. Chairman, if all the citizens of Canada were to say: Let us disobey the law, let us try to get around it; if we do not get caught, we will continue. Or else, if they said: Let us try and disobey the law, whatever it is, and even if the courts rule that we are doing wrong, we will have benefited from it during two years.
That is exactly what the C.N.R. is doing now with its trucking business in the province of Quebec. It never obtained any permit from the transport board, but it operates that business none the less.
What would you think of a private firm which would start operating a television station without having obtained a licence from the board of broadcast governors and which would say: "If we do not get a licence, we shall stop operations", while keeping on with its broadcasts. It would be surprising to see how quickly the board of broadcast governors would put a stop to such proceedings.
Under this bill, we go further than that. The people's money is given to the C.N.R. to enable it to violate the law in the province of Quebec by entering into competition with private business.
I think that the members of parliament cannot, in all conscience, vote funds to that end. That is why we are opposed to the principle of voting money to help the C.N.R. compete with the very people from whom those funds are collected. After all, this money is taken in the form of taxes from the trucking companies in the province of Quebec and handed out to the C.N.R. so that it can compete with those same companies.

Freight Rates Reduction Act
We have always claimed that this was socialism.
Mr. Chairman, socialist policy consists in imposing taxes on the people to enable the government to go into business, and once in business, it taxes the people in order to make up its own deficits. Such is socialism.
We are again asked today to vote money in order to help the government compete with private enterprise, whether such competition is illegal or not. Indeed, the C.N.R. is doing just that at present in the province of Quebec.
And we are expected to keep on voting money for the government and to take that money away from the taxpayers. We are entirely against it.
Mr. Chairman, we agreed to hasten adoption of the preceding bills, but as far as this one is concerned, we are definitely against it. If we think of what this has permitted in the past, more precisely a constant interference by the government in fields where private enterprise is doing very well, we are surely not to be expected now to help make things worse.
Mr. Chairman, legislation like this one is being passed, and we are told that they are just temporary measures for a period of only 12 months. After 12 months, we are asked again to extend their application. After a further period of 12 months, the same thing happens over again. As a matter of fact, the situation keeps repeating itself.
For how many years shall we have to vote public funds to make up the C.N.R. deficits, in addition to the $65 million this company is already getting, without mentioning the $50 million which were passed at full speed the other day?
Today we are asked to vote $25 million. Those amounts are all for the C.N.R. How long will this be kept up.
Mr. Chairman, first we must put some order in the administration of the C.N.R., otherwise, similar measures will keep coming before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The most important piece of business tomorrow, after we take third reading of the bill based on the resolution which is No. 21 on today's order paper is, of course, interim supply, so that we can get the appropriation bill through and have the other house consider it. By long odds that is the most important. The second item to which we would like to give our attention is the
Business of the House
bill based on the resolution pertaining to the world's fair. If time permits, other items of business will be called accordingly, but there will be a chance tomorrow to consult and see what progress we are making.

1 just want to make sure that I understand clearly and that the house does. I understand that third reading of the bill respecting the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act will be taken first; then we will go into committee of supply and take supply until that is completed, and then take the Montreal bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct-the world's fair bill.
